title: Janmashtami
intro: Nine verses in which Krishna speaks of who he is and why he is born, counting down to Janmashtami.

posts.caption: Janmashtami, the celebration of Krishna's birth, falls next week, and until then each day brings a verse in which Krishna speaks of who he is. Here he calls himself the source of all. The Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition, including ISKCON, treats this verse and the three after it as the essence of the whole Gita.

Krishna's image for how everything depends on him: the world strung on him like pearls on a thread. The thread is unseen, yet it holds the whole string together. Vaishnava teachers read this as a personal God sustaining all things; Advaita reads it as one reality underlying the many.

Krishna addresses Arjuna as Gudakesha, "conqueror of sleep," and names himself the self in the heart of every being. This verse opens chapter 10's long list of his vibhutis, or glories: among rivers he is the Ganga, among the immovable the Himalaya, among the Pandavas Arjuna himself.

What matters, Krishna says, is not the size of an offering but the devotion behind it. On Janmashtami, many prepare offerings for the infant Krishna, often including butter, milk sweets and tulsi leaves. Stories of his childhood raids on the butter pots earned him the name Makhan Chor, "butter thief."

Near the end of the Gita, Krishna sums up bhakti, devotion, as mind, love, worship and reverence all turned toward him, with a promise attached. Its first line repeats, almost word for word, the last verse of chapter 9. It ends on a personal note: Arjuna is dear to him.

With Janmashtami days away, a verse on how Krishna takes birth at all. He is unborn and imperishable, yet comes into the world by his own power. Shankara reads this as the Lord appearing to be born through his maya; Ramanuja and other Vaishnava teachers read it as a real birth by his own will, not bound by karma.

posts.display: Whenever there is decay of righteousness, O Bhârata, and there is exaltation of unrighteousness, then I Myself come forth.
posts.caption: Perhaps the best-known verse about the avatar, the divine "descent" into the world. Whenever dharma, the right order of things, declines, Krishna says he comes forth. Hindu tradition tells of many descents of Vishnu, with Rama and Krishna the most widely worshipped.

Why he comes: to protect the good, to end wrongdoing and to firmly establish dharma, age after age (yuge yuge). For some communities Janmashtami falls today, while many others celebrate tomorrow, as traditions follow slightly different calendar rules. Many fast and keep vigil until midnight, the traditional hour of Krishna's birth.

Happy Janmashtami. Tradition tells that Krishna was born at midnight in a prison cell in Mathura, to Devaki and Vasudeva, and was carried across the Yamuna to be raised in Gokul by Yashoda and Nanda. Here he calls his birth and deeds divine. Thank you for celebrating with us.
